      "verbatim": "Of 40 patients treated on both arms, 71.8% had a decreased slope (log(PSA)) at 24 weeks (p = 0.0012) and 74.2% had a decreased slope at 48 weeks (p = 0.0004) [38]."

    },
    {
      "statistic": "negative slope",
      "value": 15.0,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "share of patients who developed a negative PSA slope (decreasing PSA)",
      "compared": "TARP vaccine vs. baseline PSA slope in prostate cancer patients",
      "species": ["human"],
      "n": 40,
      "n_counts": "patients",
      "verbatim": "15% of the patients actually developed a negative slope, that is a decreasing PSA."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "tumor growth rate constant",
      "value": 0.5,
      "unit": "fold",
      "measures": "reduction in tumor growth rate constant",
      "compared": "TARP vaccine vs. baseline tumor growth rate in prostate cancer patients",
      "species": ["human"],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "This decreased tumor growth rate was corroborated by an independent analysis of tumor growth rate constant obtained by fitting the PSA values to an exponential growth curve [45], which found that the tumor growth rate constant fell in half (p = 0.003)."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "new response",
      "value": 77.5,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "share of patients who made a new T cell response to vaccine peptides not present at baseline",
      "compared": "TARP vaccine vs. baseline T cell responses in prostate cancer patients",
      "species": ["human"],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": "patients",
      "verbatim": "When T cell responses were measured as interferongamma ELISPOT responses to the two vaccine peptides and the wild-type version of 29–37, 77.5% of patients made a new response not present at baseline (considered positive if ≥ 3-fold over background at at least two time points and statistically significant), but the magnitude of response did not correlate with clinical response [38]."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "clinical benefit",
      "value": 45.0,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "share of evaluable patients showing clinical benefit (complete response, partial response, or stable disease lasting ≥ 6 months) at second and third dose levels",
      "compared": "HER2 adenoviral vector vaccine vs. baseline in advanced metastatic cancer patients",
      "species": ["human"],
      "n": 11,
      "n_counts": "evaluable patients",
      "verbatim": "At the lowest dose of 5 million autologous DCs, we saw no clinical responses (and no antibody responses), but at 10 and 20 million DCs, 5/11 evaluable patients, with metastatic cancers that had failed all standard therapies, showed evidence of clinical benefit (either complete response, partial response, or stable disease lasting ≥ 6 months) (Wood et al., manuscript in preparation)."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "power to discriminate among PSA responders vs non-responders",
      "value": 85.0,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "power of a combination of DC genes to discriminate between patients who responded to PSA and those who did not",
      "compared": "DC phenotype vs. PSA response in prostate cancer patients treated with TARP vaccine",
      "species": ["human"],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "By ROC curves, this gave 85% power to discriminate among PSA responders vs non-responders, and 98% power to discriminate among immunological responders and non-responders."
    },
    {
      "statistic": "power to discriminate among immunological responders and non-responders",
      "value": 98.0,
      "unit": "percent",
      "measures": "power of a combination of DC genes to discriminate between patients who had an immunological response and those who did not",
      "compared": "DC phenotype vs. immunological response in prostate cancer patients treated with TARP vaccine",
      "species": ["human"],
      "n": null,
      "n_counts": null,
      "verbatim": "By ROC curves, this gave 85% power to discriminate among PSA responders vs non-responders, and 98% power to discriminate among immunological responders and non-responders."
    }

  "headline_index": 0,
  "what_the_study_did": "The study translated two cancer vaccine strategies, one targeting prostate cancer antigen TARP and another targeting HER2, from preclinical mouse studies to human clinical trials.",
  "what_it_found": "Both vaccine strategies showed promising early results in human clinical trials, with the TARP vaccine appearing to slow tumor growth in a majority of patients and the HER2 vaccine showing clinical benefit in patients with advanced metastatic cancers.",
  "key_quotes": [
    {
      "quote": "We translated two cancer vaccine strategies from mice into human clinical trials.",
      "topic": "Translation to humans"
    },
    {
      "quote": "With no difference between arms, 74% of combined subjects had a decreased PSA slope at 1 year compared to their own baseline slopes (p = 0.0004).",
      "topic": "TARP vaccine efficacy"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Thus, cancer vaccines developed in mice were successfully translated to humans with promising early results.",
      "topic": "Overall success"
    },
    {
      "quote": "At the second and third dose levels, 45% of evaluable patients showed clinical benefit.",
      "topic": "HER2 vaccine efficacy"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Thus, the vaccine appeared to slow tumor growth in nearly ¾ of patients [38].",
      "topic": "TARP vaccine efficacy"
    },
    {
      "quote": "We conclude that both categories of cancer vaccines (targeting both arms of the adaptive immune system) can be translated from preclinical murine models to human clinical trials with promising early results.",
      "topic": "Conclusion"

  ]
